paras: The threatened lynching of George Tippett took place in February 1888 in Panola County, Texas, after Tippett, a Black barber, was jailed at Carthage when silver dollars from the robbery and murder of County Treasurer D. C. Hill were found buried at his home. Fears that he would be lynched were reported while he was held, and a later wire dispatch said he had "narrowly escaped being lynched." Suspicion then shifted to Tom Forsyth, the sheriff's son, who confessed to the murder and was himself hanged by a crowd, and wire reports said Forsyth had planted the money in the barber's yard.

Hill, the treasurer of Panola County, was killed in his office at Carthage on February 10, 1888, and more than $6,000 was reported stolen. On February 14 a Carthage correspondent wrote that a young white man arrested on suspicion had been released for lack of evidence and that "a colored barber" had been arrested that day.

According to a Longview dispatch to the Fort Worth Gazette, a child playing in the garden of the house where Tippett lived found a silver dollar, and digging turned up about a thousand more that appeared "lately and hastily buried." Tippett was arrested and held in the Carthage jail, charged, in a wire version of the story, with complicity in Hill's murder. The Gazette described him as the son of John Tippet, a Black property owner of good standing in Longview, and said the son was "almost white" but had been thought by some "a desperate and suspicious character." The same dispatch reported "considerable fears" of lynching him, while repeating a rumor that the money had been planted to direct suspicion toward him. A Texas state-news column called him "a mullatto barber" arrested at Carthage, though the surviving text of that item breaks off mid-sentence.

On February 27 officers arrested Tom Forsyth, the sheriff's son, who had long served as his father's deputy. The Gazette reported that Forsyth had been under suspicion since he found the sack of silver near Tippett's yard, and that on his arrest he tried to blame Tippett before saying, "No, he is innocent." A Longview account added that H. E. Parker, who worked up the case, had let Forsyth believe he was after Tippett while shadowing Forsyth to the hidden money. Forsyth confessed in the courthouse, and that night about 400 men took him from the jail and hanged him at Carthage.

Wire dispatches datelined "Beeville" on February 29 stated that Forsyth had tried to throw suspicion on the barber "by planting a lot of stolen money" in his yard, and that the barber had "a very narrow escape from being lynched." None of these reports describes a crowd gathering against Tippett, names anyone who threatened him, or says when he was released.

All of the surviving coverage of Tippett comes from white newspapers, and it followed the course of the Hill murder case. In mid-February the Fort Worth Gazette headlined the discovery "A Thousand Silver Dollars Found Buried in a Negro Barber's Yard," calling the find "very strong proof of his guilt," and short wire versions ran as far away as Los Angeles and Illinois. After Forsyth's arrest the barber appeared mainly as the man the sheriff's son had tried to implicate, as the Memphis Appeal, the Wichita Eagle and the Butler Weekly Times printed the "Beeville" dispatch with his name spelled Tibbetts, Tibbett and Tibbitt.

Texas papers gave far more space to Forsyth's hanging, which the Austin Weekly Statesman ran under the heading "Lynch Law," noting that no masks were worn and describing the lynchers as "about 400 of Panola county's best citizens."

Accounts differ on how the money was found: the February dispatches credit a child playing in the yard, while the Gazette's report of Forsyth's arrest says Forsyth himself found it near Tippett's yard. Only the wire sent after Forsyth's confession states outright that he planted the money; earlier the Gazette carried the idea only as a rumor. The wire's "Beeville" dateline repeats the wording of a Gazette dispatch from Beckville, where Forsyth was buried, and every account places the jail and the arrests at Carthage.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of George Tippett
bases: A Black barber jailed on suspicion of a murder and robbery was the object of lynching fears (A2) and was later said to have narrowly escaped being lynched (A9, A13); no attack on him is described.
Tippett was not killed; the papers report only fears of lynching him (A2) and a 'narrow escape' (A9, A13), with no crowd, number or act described, so this is a threatened lynching at most.

His arrest after the silver was found at his home is reported independently by the Gazette's Carthage and Longview correspondents and the Longview wire (A1, A2, A3, A4), and the danger of lynching by both the Gazette's Longview special (A2) and the separate 'Beeville' wire (A9, A13), though neither describes any crowd action.

framing.detail: The Gazette headlined 'A Thousand Silver Dollars Found Buried in a Negro Barber's Yard', called the find 'very strong proof of his guilt' yet reported that his family was respected and that the money may have been planted.
The 'Beeville' dispatch under heads like 'Charged With Murder' and 'Confessed to Murder' cast the barber as the target of Forsyth's planted evidence.
The Gazette's post-arrest specials quoted Forsyth calling Tippett innocent and reserved their fear of 'mob law' for Forsyth.

info: Barber arrested about February 14, 1888, after silver was found buried at his home; lynching fears reported by February 16; Forsyth arrested February 27 and hanged the night of February 28.
Held in the jail at Carthage, county seat of Panola County; wire datelined 'Beeville' (a parallel Gazette dispatch is datelined Beckville).
George Tippett (also Tibet, Tippet, Tibbet, Tibbett, Tibbetts, Tibbitt; 'John Tippett' in one item), a Black ('negro', 'colored', 'mullatto') barber.
Accused of complicity in the murder and robbery of County Treasurer D. C. Hill after about 1,000 silver dollars were dug up in his yard.
Not identified; no crowd against Tippett is described.
Forsyth said Tippett was innocent; Forsyth was taken from jail and hanged by about 400 men. No report of Tippett's release was found.
